items.prompt: In supervised learning, what does the training data contain?

options.label: Input features paired with known target labels
Input features only, with groups found by the model itself
States and actions, with rewards given after each action
Target labels only, with features inferred by the model

rubric: Supervised learning needs labelled examples: features plus targets.
Option 2 describes unsupervised learning; option 4 describes reinforcement learning.

items.prompt: Which term names the input variables a model uses to make a prediction?

options.label: Residuals
Features
Epochs
Labels

rubric: Features are the model inputs.
Labels are the outputs the model predicts, not the inputs.

items.prompt: Which task is an example of regression?

options.label: Predicting whether an email is spam
Predicting a handwritten digit from 0 to 9
Predicting the sale price of a house
Grouping customers into similar segments

rubric: Regression predicts a continuous number such as price.
Spam and digit prediction are classification; grouping customers is clustering.

items.prompt: What is the purpose of a test set?

options.label: To estimate performance on unseen data
To fit the model's weights by minimising the loss
To pick the features with the highest variance
To increase the amount of training data available

rubric: A test set is held out to estimate generalisation.
Fitting parameters uses the training set, not the test set.

items.prompt: Which algorithm is a clustering method?

options.label: k-means
Linear regression
Logistic regression
Naive Bayes

rubric: k-means is an unsupervised clustering algorithm.
The others are supervised methods, though logistic regression's name can mislead.

items.prompt: Which of the following are common evaluation metrics for classification models? Select all that apply.

options.label: Recall
Mean squared error
Silhouette width
Precision
Accuracy

rubric: Accuracy, precision and recall evaluate classifiers.
Mean squared error is for regression; silhouette width evaluates clustering.

items.prompt: A team has a spreadsheet of past loans. Each row lists income, loan amount and age, plus a column saying whether the borrower defaulted (yes or no). They want to predict default for new applicants. What is the target variable in this dataset?

options.label: Income, because it is the main driver of repayment
The default column
Loan amount, because it sets the size of the risk
Row number, because it identifies each applicant

rubric: The target is the outcome to predict: default.
Income, loan amount and age are features used as inputs.

items.prompt: A model scores 99% on its training data but 70% on new data. What best describes this?

options.label: Overfitting: it memorised training noise
Data leakage: test set information reached the model during training
Over-regularisation: the penalty is so strong that it blocks learning
Underfitting: it is too simple to learn the training data

rubric: A large train-test gap signals overfitting.
Underfitting would give low training scores too.

items.prompt: Why do we split data into training and test sets before evaluating?

options.label: So the model trains faster, because it only has to fit a smaller portion of the data
So the labels can be removed from the training data and the model learns without them
So that every feature has the same scale in both parts before the model is fitted
So the score reflects performance on unseen data, not memorisation

rubric: Evaluating on unseen data estimates real-world performance.
Speed and scaling are not the reason; training still needs labels.

items.prompt: What does a very high training error and a very high test error usually indicate?

options.label: Overfitting: the model memorised the noise in the training data
Underfitting: the model is too simple for the pattern
A well-fitted model that generalises correctly
Test data that leaked into the training data

rubric: Poor performance on both sets means the model fails to capture the pattern.
Overfitting shows low training error but high test error.

items.prompt: Why is a feature like 'country' (France, Japan, Brazil) usually one-hot encoded rather than coded as 1, 2, 3?

options.label: Codes 1, 2, 3 imply an order and distances that do not exist
Most models can only read binary columns, not numeric values
Integer codes discard which country each row came from
One-hot columns always let the model train faster than one column

rubric: Integer codes suggest false ordering between categories.
Models can read numbers; the issue is the implied meaning of the numbers.

items.prompt: How does unsupervised learning differ from supervised learning?

options.label: It predicts numbers while supervised predicts classes
It evaluates results using a held-out test set only
It uses labels but needs less data than supervised
It finds structure in data without target labels

rubric: Unsupervised methods work without labelled targets.
Regression versus classification is a separate distinction within supervised learning.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly explain why accuracy can mislead on a dataset with 99% negative cases? Select all that apply.

options.label: Accuracy ignores how well the rare positive class is found
Accuracy is only defined for balanced datasets
Predicting 'negative' for everything scores 99% accuracy
Accuracy rises whenever recall for positives falls

rubric: A trivial majority-class model scores high accuracy while missing all positives.
Accuracy is defined on any dataset and does not rise as recall falls.

items.prompt: A student normalises all the data using the mean and standard deviation of the whole dataset, then splits it into training and test sets. Their test score looks excellent, but the model performs worse in production. What is the best explanation?

options.label: The model was underfitted because scaling removed useful differences between feature values
Test-set statistics leaked into preprocessing, inflating the test score
Normalisation lowers performance on new data whose values differ from the training data
The test set was large enough to hide errors, so its score was not a valid estimate

rubric: Fitting the scaler on all data lets test information influence training, which is leakage.
Scaling itself does not harm; the order of steps does.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes supervised learning?

options.label: The model finds groups in data that has no target column
The model compresses features into fewer columns without any targets
The model learns by trial and error from rewards in an environment
The model learns from examples with known targets to predict new ones

rubric: Supervised learning uses labeled examples to predict targets for unseen inputs.
Distractors describe clustering, reinforcement learning and dimensionality reduction.

items.prompt: Why do we keep a test set separate from the data used for training and tuning?

options.label: It gives a final estimate of performance on data the model has not seen
It makes training faster because the model processes fewer rows overall
It lets us tune hyperparameters until the test score is as high as possible
It guarantees the model will reach higher accuracy when it is deployed

rubric: A held-out test set gives an honest estimate of generalization.
Tuning on the test set leaks information and inflates the estimate.

items.prompt: A model scores 99% accuracy on training data but 72% on validation data. What is the most likely interpretation?

options.label: The model is overfitting by memorizing noise in the training data
The model is underfitting because it has too little capacity to learn the training patterns
The model needs more features to lower its training accuracy
The validation set is too small to say anything about the model

rubric: A large train-validation gap signals overfitting.
Underfitting would show poor scores on both sets.

items.prompt: You want to predict the selling price in dollars of a house from its size and location. How should this problem be classified?

options.label: Classification, because each house belongs to one price group
Clustering, because houses with similar prices are grouped
Dimensionality reduction, because size and location are combined
Regression, because the target is a continuous numeric value

rubric: A continuous numeric target means regression.
Classification predicts discrete categories; clustering needs no target.

items.prompt: Why is feature scaling usually important for k-nearest neighbours?

options.label: It stops features with large ranges from dominating distances
It makes the chosen value of k close to optimal for the data
It reduces the influence of outliers so neighbours are more reliable
It turns categorical features into numeric ones that distances can use

rubric: k-NN relies on distances, so large-range features dominate unless scaled.
Scaling does not encode categories, remove outliers or choose k.

items.prompt: Which of the following are generally effective ways to reduce overfitting? Select all that apply.

options.label: Add regularization such as an L2 penalty
Stop training early when validation error rises
Collect more training data
Tune hyperparameters using the test set
Use a much more complex model with more parameters

rubric: More data, regularization and early stopping all limit memorization of noise.
Tuning on the test set causes leakage and added complexity usually worsens overfitting.

items.prompt: A retailer has purchase histories for 50,000 customers but no labels or categories. The marketing team wants to discover natural customer groups to tailor campaigns. Which approach fits this goal?

options.label: K-means clustering on features built from purchase histories
Linear regression to predict spending from customer age
Logistic regression to predict the segment of each customer
A decision tree trained on the existing customer categories

rubric: With no labels, unsupervised clustering finds groups.
The other options need a target or labels that do not exist.

items.prompt: A binary classifier's confusion matrix on 200 test rows is: TP=40, FP=10, FN=20, TN=130. What is its accuracy?
rubric: 0.80 is precision and 0.67 is recall, which are different metrics.

items.prompt: A classifier produces TP=45, FP=5, FN=15 on a test set. What is its recall for the positive class?
rubric: Recall = TP/(TP+FN) = 45/60 = 0.75.
0.90 is precision, which uses FP instead of FN.

items.prompt: You have a DataFrame with 400 rows and call `train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=0)`. How many rows end up in the training set?
rubric: Test size is 0.25*400 = 100, so training has 300 rows.
100 is the test set size.

items.prompt: A `city` column has 4 distinct values and you apply one-hot encoding with no dropped category. How many new columns replace `city`?
rubric: One-hot encoding makes one column per category, so 4.
3 applies only when one category is dropped.

items.prompt: You will standardize features before fitting a logistic regression model. Which sequence avoids data leakage?

options.label: Fit the scaler on the test set, then transform the train set
Fit the scaler on all the data, then split into train and test sets
Fit separate scalers on the train set and on the test set
Fit the scaler on the train set, then transform both train and test

rubric: Scaling statistics must come from training data only, then be applied to both sets.
Fitting on all data or on the test set leaks test information.

items.prompt: You are building a churn model. Which steps correctly prevent data leakage? Select all that apply.

options.label: Drop a `cancellation_date` feature that is only known after churn
Split into train and test sets before fitting the imputer
Fit the scaler only on the training rows
Scale the entire dataset first for consistency
Pick the number of neighbours by checking test-set accuracy

rubric: Preprocessing fit on training data only and removing post-outcome features prevent leakage.
Scaling everything first and tuning on the test set both leak test information.

items.prompt: A fraud model is trained on transactions where only 1% are fraud. It reports 99% accuracy on the test set, but it flags no transactions at all as fraud. You must improve its ability to catch fraud. What should you do next?

options.label: Increase the test set size until accuracy drops below 99%
Remove the fraud rows so the classes are no longer unbalanced
Report the 99% accuracy since it is already very high
Use class weights and judge the model by recall and precision

rubric: With imbalance, accuracy hides missed fraud; class weighting and recall/precision target the minority class.
Dropping fraud rows removes the signal; the other options leave the problem unaddressed.

items.prompt: A dataset has 1,000 rows. You hold out 20% as a test set, then run 5-fold cross-validation on the remaining rows. How many rows are in each validation fold?
rubric: Training pool is 800 rows, and 800 / 5 = 160 per fold.
200 ignores the test holdout; 40 divides the test set by 5.

items.prompt: A classifier produces TP=40, FP=10, FN=20, TN=130 on a test set. What is its precision?
rubric: Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 40 / 50 = 0.80.
0.67 is recall (TP / (TP + FN)), the most common mix-up.

items.prompt: You standardise features with StandardScaler before fitting a logistic regression. Which sequence is correct?

options.label: Fit the scaler on the full dataset first, then split so both parts share the same statistics
Fit the scaler on training rows only, then transform both training and test rows with it
Fit a separate scaler on the test rows so that the test features also have mean zero
Fit the scaler on the test rows only, since those are the data the model is judged on

rubric: Scaling statistics must come from training data only so no test information leaks.
Fitting on the full data leaks test statistics; a separate test scaler makes train and test inconsistent.

items.prompt: A categorical column has 5 distinct values. You one-hot encode it with `drop='first'`. How many columns does it produce?
rubric: One-hot gives 5 columns and dropping the first level leaves 4.
5 forgets the drop; 6 wrongly adds a column for missing values.

items.prompt: In 1-D k-means with k=2, the points are 1, 2, 9, 10 and the initial centroids are 1 and 2. After one assignment step and one update step, what are the centroids?

options.label: 1 and 7
1 and 2
2 and 6

rubric: Point 1 goes to centroid 1; 2, 9 and 10 go to centroid 2, giving means 1 and 7.
1.5 and 9.5 is the final result after convergence, not after one step.

items.prompt: You build a scikit-learn workflow with imputation, scaling and a model, and want an honest cross-validation estimate. Which practices are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: Fit the scaler inside each training fold and apply it to that fold's validation rows
Wrap the imputer, scaler and model in one Pipeline passed to cross_val_score
Compute imputation means on the full dataset before splitting into folds
Choose the best hyperparameters by their score on the final test set

rubric: Pipelines refit preprocessing within each fold, preventing leakage.
Full-data imputation leaks validation information, and tuning on the test set removes its independence.

items.prompt: You have 2,000 customer rows where only 3% are positive churn cases. You want an 80/20 split in which both parts keep roughly the same 3% rate, and the split must be reproducible. Which call does this?

options.label: train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=X, random_state=42)
train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, shuffle=False, random_state=42)
train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.03, random_state=42)
train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=42)

rubric: stratify=y preserves class proportions and random_state fixes the split.
stratify=X is meaningless for labels; test_size=0.03 confuses the class rate with the split size.

items.prompt: A decision tree has 100% training accuracy and 71% validation accuracy. Which diagnosis and remedy fit best?

options.label: Underfitting from heavy regularisation, so remove every constraint on the tree
Label noise in the validation set only, so retrain using the validation rows
High variance: the tree memorises noise, so limit its depth or prune it
High bias: the tree is too simple, so allow more depth to capture structure

rubric: A large train-validation gap signals overfitting (variance), fixed by constraining the model.
High bias would show poor training accuracy as well.

items.prompt: After 200 hyperparameter trials scored on one validation set, the best model scores 0.91 there but 0.84 on a fresh test set. What is the most likely explanation?

options.label: Cross-validation was skipped, and that always makes validation scores lower than test scores
Selection bias: taking the maximum over many trials overfits noise in the validation set
The model underfit the validation set, so running more trials would close the gap
The test set is too small to carry any information, so the gap is meaningless

rubric: Repeatedly choosing the best of many trials on one set inflates its score; the test set gives an unbiased value.
More trials would worsen the optimism, not reduce it.

items.prompt: A loan default model reaches AUC 0.99. Its top feature is `collections_status`, which staff fill in only after a loan has defaulted. What is the core problem?

options.label: High bias: the model is too simple, so it leans on one strong feature
Target leakage: the feature is not available at prediction time and encodes the outcome
Class imbalance: default is rare, so AUC is always close to 1 for any feature
Multicollinearity: the feature is correlated with others, which inflates the AUC

rubric: A feature recorded after the outcome leaks the label and will be unavailable in deployment.
Imbalance and collinearity do not make AUC reach 0.99 from a post-outcome field.

items.prompt: A k-NN regressor uses age (18 to 80) and annual income (20,000 to 200,000), unscaled. Accuracy is poor and barely changes if age is removed. Why?

options.label: Distance methods cannot use integer-valued features such as age, so age was effectively treated as a constant
Age is correlated with income, and k-NN removes redundant inputs before it computes any distances
k-NN automatically prunes low-variance features, so age was already dropped by the algorithm itself
Income's far larger numeric range dominates the Euclidean distance, so age hardly affects the neighbours

rubric: Unscaled features with larger ranges dominate distance; standardising fixes this.
k-NN performs no feature pruning and handles integers fine.

items.prompt: A linear regression for house price has residuals that fan out: small for cheap houses, large for expensive ones. What does this show and what is a sensible response?

options.label: Too few training rows for the model; collect more data and refit the same model
Multicollinearity among inputs; drop one feature from each highly correlated pair
Autocorrelated errors across observations; add lagged price values as extra features
Non-constant error variance; model log(price) or use weighted least squares

rubric: A funnel shape is heteroscedasticity, often reduced by transforming the target or weighting.
Autocorrelation and collinearity show different residual patterns.

items.prompt: A regression model has training error 0.30 and validation error 0.32, while the target is 0.10. Which actions address this diagnosis? Select all that apply.

options.label: Switch to a higher-capacity model such as gradient boosting
Collect many more training rows of the same kind
Add interaction or polynomial features
Increase the L2 regularisation strength

rubric: Both errors are high and close, so the model underfits and needs more capacity or expressive features.
More regularisation worsens bias, and more data rarely helps an underfit model.

items.prompt: A team predicts churn from 24 months of logs. A random 80/20 split gives AUC 0.93, but on the next month's customers after deployment AUC is 0.76. The features include rolling 90-day averages. What is the most likely cause and check?

options.label: AUC is misleading for imbalanced churn data, so report accuracy on the same random split to get a more honest estimate
Too few folds gave a noisy estimate, so move to 20-fold random cross-validation and compare the average AUC to 0.76
Random splitting leaked future information through overlapping rolling windows; re-evaluate with a time-based split
The model underfit the logs and missed real patterns, so deepen the model and rerun the same random split to confirm the gain

rubric: Random splits on time-dependent data mix future rows into training; a chronological split mimics deployment.
Other options keep the leaky random split or blame the metric.

items.prompt: A churn model scores AUC 0.93 in cross-validation but 0.71 after deployment. Features include `days_since_last_login`, computed at training time using the full customer history up to the data export date. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: Target leakage: the feature used data after the prediction point, so it encoded the outcome
Underfitting: the model was too simple to capture the churn signal, so training folds scored poorly
High variance from using too few cross-validation folds, which inflated the mean AUC across the splits
Class imbalance, which makes AUC unreliable whenever the positive class is rare in the data

rubric: Computing a feature relative to the export date leaks post-outcome information, inflating validation scores.
Underfitting would lower validation scores too; AUC is not invalidated by imbalance.

items.prompt: You standardise all features using the mean and standard deviation of the full dataset, then run 5-fold cross-validation on a regularised logistic regression. Which statement best describes the problem?

options.label: Cross-validation requires raw features, so scaled inputs change which samples land in each fold
Scaling is unnecessary for regularised models, so the step only adds noise to every fold's estimate
Standardising makes features correlated, so the coefficients become unstable across the folds
Validation folds influenced the scaling statistics, so estimates are slightly optimistic

rubric: Preprocessing fit on all data leaks validation-fold information into training.
Regularised models actually need scaling; scaling does not create correlation.

items.prompt: A random forest has training accuracy 99% and validation accuracy 82%. A linear model has 83% training and 81% validation accuracy. Which comparison is the most accurate reading?

options.label: The forest is clearly better, because its near-perfect training accuracy shows it has captured the real structure of the data more fully than the linear model
The linear model is overfitting, because its training and validation scores are so close that it must be memorising the validation set as well
The two models are equivalent, because their validation accuracies differ by under two points and so the forest's gap carries no information
The forest has a large generalisation gap, yet its validation score is slightly higher, so the gap alone does not make it worse

rubric: A large gap signals variance, but the deployed metric is validation performance.
A small gap indicates a good fit, not overfitting.

items.prompt: A model predicts house prices from features including `sqft` and `num_rooms`, which are strongly correlated. Coefficients in an unregularised linear regression flip sign when you retrain on a different sample, yet predictive error is stable. What explains this?

options.label: The model is underfitting, so coefficients are essentially random across samples
Heteroscedastic errors bias the predictions, so the coefficient signs flip from sample to sample
Multicollinearity makes individual coefficients unstable while predictions remain stable
Gradient descent failed to converge on each sample, so the fitted weights end up arbitrary

rubric: Correlated predictors share explanatory power, so coefficient estimates vary while fitted values stay stable.
Other options misattribute the cause to underfitting or optimisation.

items.prompt: In k-means on customer data with columns `age` (18-80) and `annual_income` (20,000-200,000), clusters split almost entirely by income. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: k-means always favours the feature with the highest correlation with the cluster label
Age has too few unique values, so k-means cannot use it to form clusters
Euclidean distance is dominated by the larger-scale feature, so income decides the assignment
The number of clusters is too high, which forces the split onto a single feature

rubric: Unscaled features with large ranges dominate Euclidean distance.
k-means has no labels; cluster count does not select a feature.

items.prompt: A time-series demand model shows a validation RMSE of 4.1 using random 5-fold CV, but 9.8 on the next month's real data. Which are plausible contributing causes? Select all that apply.

options.label: Random folds placed future observations in training for earlier validation points, leaking temporal structure
RMSE cannot be compared across datasets of any kind, so the two figures are meaningless
Autocorrelated neighbouring rows made validation rows near-duplicates of training rows
Demand distribution shifted after the training period, such as a new promotion pattern

rubric: Random CV on time series leaks and duplicates information, and drift hurts future data.
RMSE comparisons are valid when interpreted with context.

items.prompt: A fraud model trained on 1% positive data reaches 99% accuracy and recall of 0.05 on fraud. The team says it is excellent because accuracy is so high. The model outputs probabilities, and the default threshold of 0.5 is used. What is the best diagnosis of the situation?

options.label: The model is overfitting to the training set, so adding more trees and regularising will raise recall without changing the metric or threshold
Accuracy is dominated by the majority class and a 0.5 threshold misses most fraud; check precision-recall and tune the threshold
The 1% positive class is too small for any metric to be valid, so the evaluation must be discarded until far more fraud is collected
Accuracy of 99% shows the model separates the classes well, so the low recall is a labelling artefact that can be ignored in evaluation

rubric: A trivial majority predictor gets 99% accuracy; recall exposes the failure and thresholds can be adjusted.
Accuracy does not prove separation under imbalance.

items.prompt: You must pick a model for loan approval. Regulators require per-decision explanations, and the data is 5,000 rows of tabular features. A gradient-boosted model scores AUC 0.87, a logistic regression 0.85. Which choice best meets the criteria?

options.label: Gradient boosting, since post-hoc explanations closely track the model's true logic for each decision
Gradient boosting, since a two-point AUC gain generally outweighs the regulators' interpretability requirement
Logistic regression, since a small AUC gap is a fair price for direct, auditable explanations
A deep neural network, since it would likely beat both models on a tabular dataset of this size

rubric: Stated criteria make explainability decisive when the accuracy gap is small.
Post-hoc explanations approximate; deep nets do not reliably beat boosting on small tabular data.

items.prompt: With 300 labelled rows you want to both tune hyperparameters and report an unbiased performance estimate. Which protocol is most defensible?

options.label: Report the training score, because with only 300 rows any held-out split is too noisy to be informative
Tune with cross-validation on the whole dataset and report the best CV score, since every row is used for validation
Tune on the test set, then retrain on the training set and report the score to confirm the result
Hold out a test set for one final check and tune with inner cross-validation on the rest

rubric: Separating tuning from the final estimate avoids optimistic selection bias.
Reporting the best CV score of a tuned search is biased upward.

items.prompt: A cancer screening model must catch as many true cases as possible; a missed case is far costlier than a false alarm, and follow-up tests are cheap. Which evaluation choice best fits?

options.label: Use RMSE on predicted probabilities, since it handles asymmetric costs automatically
Maximise accuracy at the 0.5 threshold, since it weights both error types fairly
Maximise precision, since false alarms reduce trust in the screening programme
Prioritise recall and lower the threshold, accepting more false positives

rubric: Costly misses call for high recall via a lower threshold.
Accuracy and RMSE do not encode asymmetric costs.

items.prompt: A categorical feature `zip_code` has 8,000 levels across 50,000 rows. You need a robust approach for a linear model. Which option best balances overfitting risk and information retention?

options.label: Target-encode with smoothing computed within the training folds, optionally with regularisation
Drop the feature, since 8,000 levels is too many for any linear model to use without overfitting
Replace each zip with its integer label, since nearby codes tend to be geographically close and the model can use that order
One-hot encode all 8,000 levels with no regularisation, since this keeps every level's information intact

rubric: Smoothed, fold-wise target encoding keeps signal while limiting leakage and variance.
Integer labels impose false order; unregularised one-hot overfits rare levels.

items.prompt: A colleague reports that a new feature raised validation AUC from 0.810 to 0.815 on one random split of 2,000 rows. They propose shipping it, noting it adds a costly data pipeline. What is the best critique?

options.label: Ship it: the validation set is held out, so the 0.005 AUC gain is a reliable estimate of real improvement
Reject it: a gain this small on 2,000 rows cannot be detected, so no testing could justify the pipeline cost
Ship it only after checking the training AUC rose too, since that confirms the feature carries real signal
The gain is likely split noise; rerun with repeated CV and weigh it against pipeline cost

rubric: A tiny single-split difference may be noise; repeated CV and cost matter.
Rejecting features outright or calling AUC incomparable is unjustified.

items.prompt: You are choosing between random split and grouped cross-validation for a model predicting patient outcomes, where each patient has about 20 visit records. The model will be used on new patients. Which judgments are sound? Select all that apply.

options.label: Random row-level splits are preferable because each fold then has a larger, more varied training set, which gives a more reliable estimate for new patients
Grouped CV can yield a lower but more honest estimate of performance on unseen patients
Grouped CV by patient better matches deployment, since visits of one patient are highly similar
Random row-level splits can be kept if the validation score is high enough, since a high score shows the model has not memorised individual patients

items.prompt: A team must deploy a text classifier on a device with 50 ms latency and 20 MB memory. Candidates: a large transformer (F1 0.91, 400 MB, 300 ms), a distilled model (F1 0.89, 18 MB, 40 ms), and TF-IDF with logistic regression (F1 0.84, 2 MB, 2 ms). A 0.03 F1 loss is acceptable. Which should they choose?

options.label: The large transformer, because it has the best F1 and the constraints can be relaxed later
TF-IDF with logistic regression, because it is fastest and the F1 loss is unimportant
None, because no model can satisfy accuracy and latency requirements together
The distilled model, because it meets both hard limits and stays within the tolerated F1 loss

rubric: Only the distilled model satisfies latency, memory and the 0.03 F1 tolerance.
The linear model loses 0.07 F1; the transformer violates hard limits.

items.prompt: Fraud prevalence is 0.2%. Analysts can review exactly 500 transactions per day, and value comes only from fraud caught within that review queue. Which metric best compares candidate models against this criterion?

options.label: Overall accuracy at a fixed 0.5 probability threshold
Macro-averaged F1 over both classes at the default threshold
Area under the ROC curve across every possible threshold
Precision among the 500 highest-scored transactions each day

rubric: The review capacity fixes the operating point, so precision@k measures the stated value directly.
ROC AUC and accuracy reward behaviour at thresholds that will never be used; accuracy is also dominated by the majority class.

items.prompt: A weekly demand forecaster scored 8% MAPE under shuffled 5-fold cross-validation but 15% in production. Rows are weekly sales with lag and rolling-mean features. Which critique of the validation design is best justified?

options.label: MAPE is unreliable for forecasting because it is a percentage error, so the model should be re-scored with accuracy
Shuffled folds train on future weeks, so lag features leak; use rolling-origin evaluation
Shuffling hides seasonality from the model, so the folds should be stratified by calendar month to keep each season represented
Five folds is too few and leaves the variance too high, so use 20 shuffled folds to get a stable estimate

rubric: Random splits let the model see neighbouring future periods, inflating the estimate; temporal ordering must be preserved.
More folds or stratification keeps the same temporal leakage.

items.prompt: A team has 100 samples and 10,000 features. They keep the 50 features most correlated with the label using the full dataset, then run 10-fold CV on a logistic regression and report AUC 0.95. Which judgement is best?

options.label: The estimate is sound because selection only looks at feature-label correlations, not the model, so nothing about the test folds is learned
The estimate is optimistic because selection used the labels of every fold's test rows; redo selection inside each training fold
The estimate is pessimistic because 50 features is too few for 100 samples; keep 500 features so the CV AUC rises toward its true value
The estimate is sound as long as the final logistic regression is regularised with a strong L2 penalty, which shrinks any selection bias

rubric: Label-based selection before splitting leaks test information, which is severe when features far outnumber samples.
Regularisation later in the pipeline cannot undo leakage that has already occurred.

items.prompt: Model A has AUC 0.91 but overconfident probabilities; model B has AUC 0.89 and is well calibrated. A downstream system applies expected-cost thresholds directly to predicted probabilities. Which choice best fits that criterion?

options.label: Recalibrate A on a separate held-out set, keeping its ranking
Use B unchanged, because a calibrated model needs no further checks and its probabilities will stay reliable after deployment
Use A as is, because its higher AUC means its probabilities will give lower expected cost at any threshold
Use B, because a 0.02 AUC gap is within noise, so ranking quality should not influence the choice

rubric: Cost thresholds need calibrated probabilities, and monotone recalibration preserves A's better ranking.
Raw AUC ignores calibration; calibration can drift, so B's status isn't permanent.

items.prompt: An analyst tuned 500 hyperparameter configurations against one fixed 2,000-row validation set and reports the best score as the expected production performance, a 0.5% gain over the baseline. What is the strongest critique?

options.label: A 0.5% gain is within rounding error, so no validation set of this size can show any real improvement over the baseline
A 2,000-row validation set is too small to rank configurations, so the search should be rerun with a much larger validation split
Grid-style search over many configurations is invalid for tuning, so the score is void unless the search is rerun as a random search
The best score is optimistically biased by selection; confirm on untouched test data or use nested CV

rubric: Picking the maximum over many noisy evaluations inflates the score; an unused test set gives an unbiased estimate.
Search strategy and a fixed gain threshold do not address selection bias.

items.prompt: A report ranks features by permutation importance on a held-out set, where several features are strongly correlated. Which criticisms are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: Correlated features can split or mask importance, so each may look less important than the group
Permuting one feature creates unrealistic combinations, which can distort the scores
High importance proves removing the feature would lower performance after retraining
Permutation importance cannot be computed on held-out data
The ranking shows predictive reliance of the model, not causal effect on the outcome

rubric: Correlation masks importance, permutation breaks joint structure, and importance is not causal.
A retrained model could use correlated substitutes, so importance does not prove removal hurts.

items.prompt: A new recommender improves offline NDCG by 4% on logged clicks, but an online A/B test shows flat click-through. The logs were produced entirely while the old recommender chose what users saw. Which judgement best explains the gap and what to do?

options.label: Logged clicks are biased toward items the old model showed, so use counterfactual estimators or online tests
The A/B test likely lacked power to detect a 4% lift, so trust the offline metric and ship the new model
NDCG ignores rating magnitude on recommendations, so re-evaluate the new model offline using RMSE on ratings
The new model overfit the logged clicks, so add more layers and retrain to fit those clicks even better

rubric: Logs reflect exposure under the old policy, so offline gains may not transfer; counterfactual evaluation or live tests correct for it.
Dismissing the A/B test or adding capacity ignores the exposure bias.

items.prompt: A churn model's true labels arrive 60 days after prediction, but drift must be caught within a week. Which monitoring design meets both constraints?

options.label: Wait for 60-day labels, then compute accuracy on each cohort and alert when it drops below the validation baseline
Weekly checks of input and score distributions, plus performance on labelled cohorts as they mature
Retrain every night on the newest data and treat a falling training loss as proof the model is healthy
Track only the weekly mean predicted churn rate, since labels arrive too late to matter for drift detection

rubric: Label-free proxies give fast warnings while delayed labels confirm real performance.
Waiting misses the one-week requirement; mean score alone and training loss are weak signals.

items.prompt: You have 300 labelled rows and 20 features, must tune regularisation strength and report an honest generalisation estimate, and cannot reserve a separate test set. Which design satisfies this?

options.label: One 5-fold CV, tuned on all folds, reporting the best fold's score
Nested cross-validation with tuning in the inner loop and scoring on outer folds
Tune on the training score, then report CV accuracy of the chosen setting
A single 90/10 split, tuning and scoring on the 10% part

rubric: Nested CV separates tuning from evaluation so the estimate stays honest with little data.
The other options reuse the same data for selection and scoring, or give a noisy tiny holdout.

items.prompt: A dataset has many images per patient, and the positive class is 3% of patients. You need a split that avoids patient leakage and keeps similar positive rates in every fold. Which design meets both?

options.label: Random 80/20 image split repeated 10 times, averaging the scores to cut variance
Shuffled k-fold on images, stratified by image label so each fold keeps 3% positives
Stratified group k-fold, patient as group, patient label as stratum
Group k-fold by patient with no stratification, relying on large folds to balance positives

rubric: Grouping prevents the same patient appearing in both train and test, while stratification keeps rare positives balanced.
Image-level splits leak patient identity; plain grouping can leave folds with few positives.

items.prompt: A categorical feature with 40,000 levels is target-encoded using the full training set, and the model overfits badly. The fix must keep the feature's signal and not leak labels. Which fix meets this?

options.label: Replace the feature with a per-row unique index so the model cannot memorise any single category
Encode with the per-level target mean on the full training set, then add Gaussian noise to the output
Out-of-fold target encoding, smoothed toward the global mean, fitted inside each training fold
Compute the per-level target means on the held-out test set so levels match the deployment data

rubric: Out-of-fold encoding stops a row's own label shaping its feature, and smoothing stabilises rare levels.
Noise alone still leaks, and the other options destroy the signal or leak test labels.

items.prompt: A classifier trained at 10% prevalence will run where prevalence is 2%. A missed positive costs 20 times a false alarm. Which plan satisfies the cost and prevalence constraints?

options.label: Keep the 0.5 threshold, since training prevalence defines the best cutoff
Use the training-time probabilities as they are and flag cases above 20/21, since a miss costs 20 times an alarm
Oversample positives to 50% prevalence, retrain, and then use the 0.5 threshold
Recalibrate to the 2% prior, then flag cases above 1/21 probability

rubric: Cost-optimal threshold is cost_FP/(cost_FP+cost_FN) = 1/21 on probabilities matching deployment prevalence.
Reversing the threshold or ignoring the prior shift gives wrong decisions.

items.prompt: A proposed pipeline retrains a model weekly and auto-deploys it whenever accuracy on a random validation split beats the current model. Which additions are needed to make it safe? Select all that apply.

options.label: Increase model complexity each week so accuracy keeps rising
Validate incoming data schema and distributions before training
Use canary deployment with automatic rollback on metric regression
Compare challenger and current model on the same recent holdout
Shuffle all history together so the newest data has no special role

rubric: Fair comparison, data validation and staged rollout address the missing safeguards.
Growing complexity and shuffling away recency add risk without safety.

items.prompt: A lender needs a credit model with 200 tabular features, nonlinear interactions, and scoring under 50 ms. Regulators require intrinsic interpretability, with no post-hoc explanation tools. Which design meets every constraint?

options.label: A logistic regression on raw features with no interaction terms, using L1 regularisation to keep it sparse
A 1,000-tree boosted model explained afterwards with SHAP values for each decision
A generalised additive model with a few validated pairwise terms
A deep neural network with attention maps shown to regulators for each score

rubric: An additive model with limited interactions is intrinsically interpretable, fast, and captures key nonlinearity.
SHAP and attention are post-hoc; plain logistic regression ignores required interactions.
